ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Policy for new Industries 
*401.  SHRI ONWARD L. NONGTDU: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government have formulated any short -term and long - 
erm policy to set-up new industries in industrially backward districts of the 
country; 
(b) if so, the details of initiatives taken by Government since 1991; 
and 
(c) the total amount provided by Government for establishment of 
industries in these backward districts during the Eighth and Ninth Plan? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MININISTRY OF 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN): (a) to (c) A Statement is 
laid on the Table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
(a) and (b) The Indu strial Policy of 1991 aims inter alia to spread 
industrialisation to backward areas of the country through institutions, 
appropriate initiatives and infrastructure investments that would facilitate 
and "enable" private investment. The initiative for industrial development of 
backward areas thus lies primarily with State Govts. The Union Govt, 
supplements their efforts through various schemes and incentives. Whereas 
fiscal incentives for setting up industrial units constitute the short term 
policy, efforts f or the development for industrial infrastructure to attract 
industries - being primarily long gestation schemes - characterise the long 
term policy. The important initiatives taken by the Central Govt, for 
promotion of industries in backward areas througho ut the nation in the areas 
of infrastructure development and fiscal incentives are set out below. For the 
North East a separate policy package was announced in December, 1997 (set 
out, thereafter) 
1 

RAJYA SABHA 24 APRIL, 2000 
Policy Initiatives 
Infrastructural Development 
(1) The Ministry of Small Scale Industries, and Agro and Rural 
Industries is implementing the Integrated Infrastructure 
Development Scheme (IID). The scheme envisages 
development of infrastructure facilities for small industries to 
facilitate location of industries in rural/backward areas. 
(2) The following two Schemes though announced before 1991 are 
ongoing schemes of the Ministry of Commerce and Industry in 
the Eighth and Ninth Five Year Plans: 
(i) Growth Centre Scheme: Under this scheme 71 gro wth centres are 
proposed to be developed throughout the country which would 
be provided with basic infrasturcture facilities like power, water, 
telecommunication, sewage, effluent disposal etc. enabling them 
to attract industries. 
(ii) Transport Subsidy Sc heme: This Scheme was introduced in July, 
1971 to promote industries in hilly, remote and inaccessible 
areas. Under the scheme, subsidy ranging from 50% -90% is 
admissible on transport costs incurred on movement of raw 
materials and finished goods from desi gnated rail heads/ports 
upto the location of the industrial units. 
(3) Fiscal Incentives: Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue  
has notified 123 Industrially Backward districts classified as  
Category A and Category B, [vide Notification No. 714(E), da ted 
7-10-1997] for grant of tax concession under Income Tax Act, 
1961, 
(i) Industrially backward States and Union Territories in 
Schedule Eight of the Income Tax Act, 1961 are also entitled to 
an identical benefit for undertakings set up on or before 31- 3-
2002 as per Finance Bill, 2000. 
(4) Industrial Policy Package for North East: Considering its  
peculiar geographical problems and continued backwardness, a 
new Industrial Policy and other concessions were announced for  
the North East region in December, 1997.

Import Restrictions on Food and Allied Products 
*403. DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY: Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) Whether it is a fact that Government propose to lift import 
restrictions on food produce and allied products, including milk and milk 
products; 
(b) Whether it is also a fact that the measure would adversely affect 
millions of Indian farmers; and 
(c) If so, what rem edial steps Government propose to take in the 
interest of agricultural and dairy community? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI OMAR ABDULLAH) : (a) to (c) A statement is 
laid on the table of the House. 
STATEMENT 
Import restrictions on various items including food produce and allied 
products and milk and milk products are being removed as part of the import 
liberalisation programme of the government and also in terms of our 
international obligations. 
However, all imports in the country are subject to applicable rates of 
customs duties and are also subject to domestic laws, rules, orders, 
regulations, technical specifications, environmental and safety norms as 
applicable to domestically produced goods. This should provide adequate 
protection to domestic farmers. 
10 

24 APRIL, 2000 RAJYA SABHA 
India's tariff bindings at W.T.O. for most of the agricultural items are 
fairly high and effective rates of customs duties can be raised to those levels, 
in case there is any evidence of substantial increase in imports. 
In the Budget for the year 2000 -2001, presented before the Parliament, 
import duties on many of the agricultural items, (Chapter 1 to 24) of ITs 
(HS) Classification of Export and Import Items, have been increased to 
provide further protection to domestic farmers, e. g. duty on rice has been 
increased from 0% to upto 80%, on maize from 0% to 50%, on apples from 
35% to 50%. 
The imports are being closely monitored and Government is 
determined to ensure through appropriate use of  the tariff mechanism that 
imports do not cause any serious detriment or injury to the domestic farmers.

Protest against New Export-Import Policy 
*408. SHRI VAYALAR RAVI: Will the Minister of COMMERCE  
AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state : 
(a) whether any State Government has made a protest against the New 
Export Import policy; 
(b) if so, what are the reasons given in the protest; and 
(c) the reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
MURASOLI MARAN) 
(a) to  (c) The State Government of Kerala has expressed certain 
reservations regarding removal of QRs on 714 items which may affect the 
economy of the State of Kerala as well as the Country. According to them, 
many items on which QRs have n ow been removed are in the category of 
processed foods and consumer items including items of daily use such as salt 
and tapioca which may affect the local manufacturers/producers of these 
items. In addition, the State Government has also expressed the view that free 
importability of luxuary items may lead to conspicuous expenditure and 
reduce the domestic savings. 
The Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) were being maintained ever since 
1974 on balance of payment (BOP) grounds. The Quantitative Restrictions 
were being removed progressively in line with the policy of import 
liberalisation. However, with the improvement in the BOP position, certain 
members of the WTO had disputed the need to continue with QRs for BOP 
reasons. India could negotiate with most of the trading partners with the 
exception of USA for phasing out these QRs. USA filed a dispute and the 
Dispute Settlement Panel constituted in November, 1997 ruled against India. 
India filed an appeal before the Appellate Body of WTO against the findings 
of the  Panel but the Appellate Body also upheld the findings of panel. 
Consequently, under an agreement signed between India and USA, QRs on 
714 items have been removed with effect from 1 -4-2000 and those on the 
remaining 715 items are to be removed by 1- 4-2001. The QRs in respect of 
these 1429 tariff lines were withdrawn preferentially for imports from 
SAARC countries w.e.f. 1st August, 1998. 
28 

24 APRIL, 2000 RAJYA SABHA 
The customs duties on most of the items for which QRs have been 
removed, has already been raised to the peak level of 35%. On some 
agricultural items like rice, duty has been raised in the case of rice upto 80%, 
on apples to 50% and on maize to 50%. The imports are being closely 
monitored and Government is determiend to ensure through appropria te use 
of tariff mechanism that imports do not cause any serious detriment or injury 
to the domestic producers. Moreover, in the event of any unfair trade 
practice being adopted by exporters of other countries or if there were to be a 
sudden surge in impor ts causing injury to the domestic industry, sufficient 
provisions are available in the form of anti -dumping/safeguard measures to 
protect the domestic industry.

Patenting of Indian Plants 
3085. SHRI RAMDAS AGARWAL : Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state : 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the news -item 
captioned "Made in Indian plants get patented abroad", published in the 
Hindustan Times, dated 6th April, 2000; 
(b) whether it is a fact that Karela (Bittergourd), Jamun (Blackberry) 
and Baigan (Brinjal) etc., grown and widely used in India for centuries,  are 
going to be patented in countries like Japan, U.S. and China; 
59 

RAJYA SABHA 24 APRIL, 2000 
(c) if so, whether India now face the situation of having to pay royalty 
for using our own natural resources; and 
(d) by when Government propose to bring forward suit able legislation 
to fill this huge loophole? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (DR. RAMAN) : (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) and (c) Patents cannot be granted for products existing in nature as 
they would not meet the criteria of patentability, namely, novelty, inventive 
step and industrial applicability. However, patents have reportedly been 
granted on compositions based on certain properties of plants. 
Patents are granted under the sovereign prerogative of countries 
according to their respective Patent Laws and have territorial effect that is, 
they are effective only in the country of grant. However, as and when 
information is received about patents being obtained on certain items which 
are not considered patentable and which affect Indian i nterests, steps are taken 
to assess whether the grant of such patent can be challenged under the patent 
laws of the country concerned. 
As the patents have territorial effect and are valid only in the country of 
grant, therefore, the question of paying any royalty for using our natural 
resources does not arise. 
(d) In order to protect bio- resources, the Patents (Second Amendment) 
Bill 1999, contains provisions for madatory disclosure of source and 
geographical origin of the biological material used in the in vention while 
applying for patents in India. Provisions have also been incorporated to 
include the non- disclosure or wrongful disclosure of the same as grounds for 
opposition and for revocation of the patent, if granted. Provisions in this 
regard are contained in clauses 8, 17 and 28 of the said Bill. 
In order to protect traditional knowledge from being patented, 
provisions have been incorporated in the Patents (Second Amendment) Bill, 
1999 to include anticipation of invention by available local knowledge, 
including oral knowledge, as one of the grounds for opposition as also for 
revocation of patent. Provisions in this regard are contained in clauses 17 and 
28 of the said Bill. 
Apart from this Government has also initiated an exercise to develop a 
digital data base of traditional knowledge in the field of medicinal plants to 
aviod patenting of such knowledge.

interdependent world: applying the lessons of the past to make globalisation 
an effective instrument for the development of all countries and all people". 
The Conference adopted two documents viz. 
(i) The Bangkok Declaration : A political declaration on the experience 
of globalisation, liberalisation and the future role of UNCTAD; and 
(ii) The Plan of Action : An outline of the work programme of UNCTAD 
for the next four years. This document has two parts. Part -I is an 
analytical section on evaluation of the developmental impact of 
globalisation while Part- II deals with UNCTAD's engagement 
highlighting inter-alia issues relati ng to international trade, 
investment, enterprise, and transfer of technology.

The Bangkok Declaration states that in the context of the opportunities 
created by globalisation, the paramount objectives of the endeavours of al l 
countries have been the promotion of growth and sustainable development 
and the quest for equity and participation by all. In this context, the 
Conference called for more effective coordination and cooperation among 
Governments and among international institutions in dealing with global 
interdependence and development. The opportunities, challenges and the 
risks of globalisation were discussed and it was felt that globalisation raises 
the risk of marginalisation of countries particularly the poorest countries and 
the most vulnerable groups everywhere. The Conference noted that solidarity 
and a strong sense of moral responsibility must be the guiding light of 
national and international policy as they are prerequisites for prosperous, 
peaceful and secure world based on true partnership.

National Housing & Habitat Policy of 1998 was laid on the Table of Lok 
Sabha and Rajya Sabha on 29th July, 1998. The National Housing & Habitat 
Policy envisages Governments role as an enabler rather than a builder. 
Government regulatory, technical and financial constraints facing the Housing

providing affordable shelter for all in rural areas  within a specified time frame

URBAN EMPLOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to 
state the details of the schemes that are being formulated for the resettlement 
of slum dwellers ? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA) : Presently the 
National Slum D evelopment Programme (NSDP) which was introduced in 
August, 1996 to provide Additional Central Assistance (ACA) to States/UTs 
for the development of urban slums is under imlementation. The ACA 
released under this scheme can be utilised to provide physical amenities like 
water supply, storm water drains, community infrastructure, community 
primary health care, social amenities like pre- school education, adult 
education, maternity and child health and primary health care etc. It also has a 
provision for shelter upgradation. 
A draft National Slum Policy has been prepared to address the problem 
of holistic development of slums. The policy embodies the core principle that 
households in all urban informal settlements should have access to certain 
basic minimum ser vices irrespective of land tenure or occupancy status. The 
main objectives are to create awareness amongst the Public and Government 
to bring about the integration of the settlements and the communities residing 
within them into the urban areas as a whole.  To strengthen the legal and 
policy framework to facilitate the process of slum development and 
improvement on a sustainable basis. And lastly to establish a framework for 
involving all stakeholders for the efficient and smooth implementation of 
Policy obj ectives. The draft Policy have been sent to all States for their 
comments.

(c) what steps have been taken to contain migration from rural areas 
to urban areas ? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN EMPLOYMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION (SHRI SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA) : (a) So far as 
Ministry of Urban Employment & Poverty Alleviation is concerned no census 
survey has been undert aken. However,Planning Commission had provided a 
statement on 'Estimate of Poverty' (1993- 94) according to which number of 
persons below poverty line in Urban Areas is 763.37 lakhs. 
(b) No, Sir. This Ministry has launched a Urban Poverty Alleviation 
Programme called Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rojgar Yojna (SJSRY) only with 
effect from 01-12-97, as yet no assessment has been made. 
(c) Ministry of Rural Areas & Employment had reported that they are 
implementing the programme of Swarnjayanti Gram Swarozgar Yojana 
(SGSY) aimed at creating Self -employment opportunities for the rural poor. 
Further in order to create wage employment opportunities in the rural areas, 
that Ministry implements the Employment Assurance Scheme. 
The SGSY was launched with effect from 1st April, 1999 . SGSY is 
conceived as a holistic programme of micro enterprises covering all aspects of 
self-employment viz. Organisation of the rural poor into self -help groups 
(SHGs) and their capacity building, planning of activity clusters, 
infrastructure build up, t echnology, credit and marketing. Assistance is 
provided to rural poor families below proverty line through a mix of bank 
credit and subsidy from Government. 
Employment Assurance Scheme (EAS) was launched on 2nd October, 
1993 for implementation in selected blocks. Over the years scheme was 
extended to all the blocks of the country. At present, all the districts of the 
country are covered under the scheme. The primary objective of the EAS is 
creation of additional wage employment opportunities during the lean  
agricultural season through manual work for the rural poor living below the 
poverty line. The secondary objective is the creation of durable community, 
social and economic assets and sustained employment and development. 
It is expected that such steps in rural areas will discourage migration to 
urban areas.

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
Recognition of the Janakinath Bhavan, Cuttck where Netaji Subhas 
Chandra Bosewas born as National Monument 
DR. C. NARAYANA REDDY (Nominated): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I 
seek your kind permission to bring to the notice of this august House, a very 
vital item that warrants immediate consideration and follow -up action. This 
special mention relates to the place of birth of Netaji Subhas Chandra Bose. If 
asked to name three greatest national leaders of the 20th Century who played 
the most exemplary role in the attainment of freedom, the unanimous choice of 
the country would be Gandhiji, Nehruji and Netaji. Their births were indeed 
great events in the annals of the nation and their birth- places stand as 
magnificent memorials. The buildings in Porbandar and Allahabad where 
Gandhiji and Nehruji were born,  respectively, are held in high esteem and 
kept to serve as sources of inspiration to the present as well as future 
generations. 
184 

[24 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
In my view, such places and memorials are treasures to be proud of. 
They are an integral part of our cultural heritage. And culture is the identity of 
a nation. It expresses the aspirations of the people. 
The enlightened members of the House know that Netaji was born in 
1897 in a two -storey building now called Jankinath Bhavan in Oriya Bazar, 
Cuttack, Orissa. The building is not yet declared as a National Monument. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, it pains me to inform that according to reliable 
sources of information, the building is now in a state of collapse. I may be 
permitted to briefly recall the history o f the building so that the House may 
share my anxiety. Netaji's father Janakinath Bose constructed the building on 
a one-acre plot. When the family moved to Calcutta, the building was given to 
their relatives. After more than five decades of its constructi on, the relatives 
wanted to sell it off. The State Government did rightly purchase it. Dr. 
Harekrushna Mahtab, the then Chief Minister of Orissa, established the "Netaji 
Subhas Sadan Trust" and transferred the building to the Trust. As a tribute to 
Netaji, a Maternity Centre was started in the building on behalf of the Trust. 
Sir, it is learnt that due to lack of funds, the staff are not getting their salaries 
regularly. Though the Chief Minister is the ex officio President of the Trust, it 
does not have ad equate resources. As such, the building is still in a 
dilapidated condition. Only a part of the roof was repaired. The remaining part 
is about to collapse. It appears that there was some technical objection from the 
Archaeological Survey of India for repla cing the roof, and the Public Works 
Department was not in favour of repair, as it would cost more. 
While such was the state of the building, the recent super cyclone 
caused further damage to it. According to estimates, the restoration of the 
Janakinath Bhavan would cost around Rs.5 crores. In this connection, I must 
congratulate hon. Member, Justice Ranganath Misraji, for allotting Rs.5 lakhs 
from his MPLADS funds for the repairs. If the authorities consider that I can 
be of assistance in the endeavour, I am prepared to offer a token amount of 
Rs.5 lakhs from my MPLADS funds, as a Member of the Rajya Sabha, 
nominated by the President of India. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, is it not our responsibility to put in all efforts and 
restore the memorial? It will be an act of  homage to Netaji, if this building is 
recognized as a National Monument and necessary funds are sanctioned for 
its repair and restoration.   In the context of the eminence of Netaji Subhas 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [ 24 April, 2000] 
Chandra Bose as a national lead er, it will be in the fitness of things that the 
Archaeological Survey of India takes up the issue, without any further loss of 
time, to get the building declared as a monument of national importance and 
maintain it as a Centrally -protected monument. It ha s already 3593 such 
monuments under its maintenance. Further, we have also a scheme for the 
development and maintenance of National Memorials. 
I reiterate the urgency of the matter, in view of the deteriorating 
condition of the building associated with Netaji. The building is a part of our 
great cultural heritage and we are very much proud of it, and equally anxious 
to protect and preserve it. 
Here, I am reminded of the episode of the Winter Palace of Soviet 
Russia in Leningrad. It was one of the greatest architecutural monuments built 
by the Czars. It was destroyed during the October Revolution. Though it was 
built by the Czar rulers, the Communist Government rebuilt it, keeping in 
view its importance as a monument. I was told, during my visit to Leningrad 
in 1980, that the new Government was against the rule of Czar, but not against 
their architectural creations. 
I do not want to draw a comparison between the two buildings. Only 
the element of importance of the monument is relevant here. The Winter 
Palace h ad architectural grandeur. The Janakinath Bhavan has national 
importance. 
Mr. Chairman, Sir, it has become customary on the part of 
Governments to make promises on occasions of Jayanthis or Vardhanthis of 
national leaders to do everything to fittingly comm emorate their glory. The 
successive Governments also do not lag behind in endorsing the promises in 
tune with the occasions. Promises speedly flow, but results are very slow. I 
have tried to depict the difference between the promise and practice in one of 
my Urdu Gazals. I quote:- 
इस शेर में िसनारे मेरा तकल्लुस है ।

I conclude, by reiterating my request to the hon. Minister of Human 
Resource Development to initiate immediate measures in this important 
matter of national significance. Thank you.

DR. M.N. DAS : Sir, I am grateful to you for giving me permission 
to associate myself with the sentiments expressed by Dr. Reddy. Sir, the whole 
of India feels proud of Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose. But the people of Orissa 
have more reasons to feel proud of him because he was born in the city of

in schools in Orissa. After 16 years of his early life when he migrated to 
Calcutta to receive higher education, again and again, in every vacation and 
holiday he made it a point to come to Cuttack to stay in his parental house. Sir, 
the house where he was born about 104 years ago, was built much earlier and 
is now in a dilapidated condition. Thousands of students from all parts of 
Orissa have made it a place of pilgrimage and come there to see the place 
where Netaji was born. Sir, many people from Orissa joined the Azad Hind 
Fauz outside India when Netaji took up the sword against the British 
Government. Many of them died. Sir, I have collected much information as a 
humble student of history. I was collecting i nformation about his childhood in 
Cuttack as to how many places he used to visit, how he used to serve the sick 
people and even cholera patients, how he used to take them to hospitals and 
how many young people felt inspired by his dedicated service to the people 
there. Sir, I would like to inform you and to the House that when Netaji Bose 
was only nine years old, he imbibed the spirit of nationalism during the 
Swadesi Movement in the city of Cuttack itself from local leaders, from his 
teachers and from his senior colleagues. There are many things. His house now 
resembles, I should not say, a ghost's house. It is in a pathetic condition. It may 
collapse anytime. We visit that place every year on the day of his birth. Unless 
the Government of India and the Mem bers of Parliament collectively come 
forward to perpetuate the memory of this bravest of the brave sons of India, the 
house of his birth will disappear once and for all. How to perpetuate the 
memory of Netaji at the very place of his birth where he spent 1 6 years of his 
life? I associate myself with the sentiments expressed by the other hon. 
Members. I appeal to all the Member of the House and to the Minister of 
Culture to kindly take up this issue seriously and see to it that the place of his 
birth is preserved and a new monument is erected there in order to inspire the 
future generations by recollecting the great achievements of Netaji.   Thank 
you.

Need to Develop India as Maritime Power 
SHRI EDUARDO FALEIRO (Goa): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I thank you 
for giving me an opportunity to bring to the notice of the House and of the 
Government the importance of the oceans and the maritime area around our 
country. India is not a small country. India is a major country in the world. 
Therefore, we must pay attention to what is happening in the oceans. Sir, what 
is happening in the oceans is this. With the advancement in technology, the 
tremendous amount of resources which are t here in the oceans have now 
become economically exploitable. While the population on land is increasing 
and the resources on land are getting less and less, to satisfy billions and 
billions of people, the industrialized countries are working in the same ma nner 
as they worked in the 19th century. So far as colonization of the land is 
concerned, because of the technological advancement, colonization did take 
place in the 19th century. Now by same reason of technological advancement, 
they want to take over the  oceans. In order that history may not repeat itself, 
the 18th and the 19th centuries may not repeat themselves, the UN announced 
the year 1998 as 'The International Year of the Oceans, so that the resources 
of the oceans could be equitably utilized for the benefit of the entire mankind. 
Also, with the support of the U.N. and the UNESCO, an independent 
World Commission was appointed, and I was appointed on behalf of the 
Government of India, if I may respectfully submit, as a member of the 
Commission. The Re port of the Commission was presented by me to hon. 
Prime Minister, Shri Vajpayee. The question that I am posing here is: What 
action has the Government of India taken in that regard? The point I am 
making now is this. India must have an Ocean Policy, just like other major 
countries have. What is happening at the moment is that the affairs 
concerning oceans are divided amongst various Ministries. You have the 
Surface Transport Ministry looking after Shipping. You have the Defence 
Ministry looking after the C oast Guard. You have the Finance Ministry 
looking after Customs. You have the Environment Ministry looking after 
Environment. Every single Ministry is involved and there is no coordination 
whatsoever. Now, my first appeal to the Government is that a Mariti me 
Council should be constituted with the Prime Minister as its head, putting all 
 193 

RAJYA SABHA [ 24 April, 2000] 
these Ministries together, and it should meet at least twice a year to formulate, 
advance and also monitor the implementation of our Mar itime Policy. The 
second thing which the Government of India must do, -all the major countries 
in the world and also some of our neighbours, for that matter, Pakistan, Iran 
and other countries, have done that - is that it should implement the London 
Convention of 1972 Protocol which purposes to control all sources of marine 
pollution and prevent pollution of sea through regulation of dumping of waste 
materials. May I say one thing from my personal experience? Once upon a 
time I was a diver, and I have gone through all the coasts, both the Eastern and 
the Western Coasts, of India. And I found that all the corals in the various 
coasts of India were dead. There are no living corals any more anywhere on 
the coast of India except in Lakshadweep and Andaman & Nicob ar Islands. 
That is a very sad thing, and this is because of pollution. We must implement 
the London Convention Protocol to control pollution just like all the other 
major countries of the world have done. The third suggestion that I am making 
is introduct ion of maritime studies in Indian universities, particularly, in 
Mumbai, Chennai and Calcutta, and for that matter, in Cochin and Goa, which 
are nearer to the sea. There is a tremendous scope for employment through 
Merchant Navy. As far as maritime studies  are concerned, we have different 
subjects. I don't want to take the time of the House in mentioning the names. 
Then, importantly, please encourage coastal shipping. Countries which have a 
tremendous amount of money, like Germany and others, develop coasta l 
shipping. Use ships and boats as a means of transportation. They are much 
cheaper because they use much less oil than railways and motors and they are 
much more environment-friendly because they don't have all those fumes 
going into the lungs of the people because of which people suffer from all 
types of respiratory diseases. I would request the Government to be alert to 
what the big powers are doing as far as the seas are concerned. Exploit 
exclusive economic zone of India which consists of more than 3 m illion 
square kilometres. You must have a comprehensive ocean policy by bringing 
together all these disparate Ministries which, at the moment, are dealing with 
our coasts and seas. Thank you.

this Address, the particular reference to the 'fixed term' is missing. I do not 
know why this omission. The other day, while speaking on the subject and

Congress Party has opposed to the setting up of a Commission to review the

document. Madam, social justice is the soul of our Constitution. Therefore, in

manifestoes of their particular parties, or quote poems of their particular 
partymen. This is what is mentioned in this volume which has come out. I 
wish the hon. Leader of the Opposition had, at least, glanced through this 
particular volume which has been withdrawn and he would not have felt so 
bad about it. 
The entire mandate  given by the then Prime Minister of putting in 
documents and proving it to the world that it is the Indians who have wrested 
independence on their own, has been completely belied and that entire 
exercise was supposed to be done by this team. I am not talk ing about their 
political affiliations and their political ideologies. 
Then, I was shocked to hear the Leader of the Opposition saying in 
this House that we are supporting Dara Singh. Who can ever support any 
murder? We in this country have been taught to hate the crime, not the 
criminal. I would tike...(Interruptions) 
THE LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION (DR. MANMOHAN 
SINGH): This is not what I said. I did not say that the BJP Member of 
Parliament offered assistance to defend Dara Singh. Can you deny this fact?  
SHRI B.P. SINGHAL: No; no. What is wrong with that. After all, a 
court has to offer a counsel, in case a man doesn't have a counsel. A counsel 
has to be given. What is wrong with that? But the individual Member's action 
cannot be considered as a party policy . I think the Leader of the Opposition is 
very well aware of that. 
Another point of controversy is this. Our Leader of the Opposition 
has emphasised that this Government or the party prevented the shooting of 
"Water". When something happens for the first t ime, it is called "an accident". 
When it happens for the second time, it is called "a coincidence". When it 
happens for the third time, repeatedly, it is called "a design". Here, I would like 
to bring to your notice that in 1991, the very lady, Deepa Mehta , wanted to 
shoot a film called "Days and Nights in Calcutta".  In 1991,  the 
214 

[24 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
then Government refused permission to her because, in the first place, that 
denigrated Calcutta and the widows of Calcutta, in particular, and the 
womenhood of India, in general. In 1993, permission was granted. But can 
you imagine the nature of the subject that was covered by the text, which was 
authorised in the 1993 sanction for the filming of "Days and Nights in 
Calcutta". I will put across on ly one specimen. I don't want to waste the time 
of the House. On page 113, it reads, "Food is shown as being put in gutters 
where beggars are waiting for it along with cows and dogs." This may be 
deleted. That was the recommendation. This is the kind of subject that Deepa 
Mehta was wanting to film in 1991. Then, she produced a film in the name of 
"Fire" and used the names of Radha and Sita for showing lesbianism. That 
was the second attempt to show what the West glorifies. The West glorifies 
lesbianism. The  West glorifies homosexuality which they may be doing, 
through parade in Los Angeles and other cities. They may glorify it. They 
may try to justify it saying, "we are not doing anything particularly immoral 
when even in India, which is supposed to be a set  of people with high moral 
values, this kind of a thing goes on". You just put up any theory and it will go 
on. That is the kind of attempt that was made by this film -maker. The third 
attempt was made when she was out to make "Water". As it happened, there  
was a rape scene, which, of course, was not shot. The rapist is known as one 
Narayana, and the name of the widow, who has been raped, is Janaki. Again, 
the names of our Gods and Goddesses were being used, despite the protest 
that took place at the time of  "Fire". If that is the audacity of a foreign film -
maker, I am ashamed that there are people in our country to support her. It is 
a shame to support people who are out to defame the women of our country. I 
would like all the Members sitting here to kindly take note of this. This was 
not the first occasion. This was the third occasion, the third attempt, to 
denigrate the women of India and the sacred city of Varanasi. In the first 
place, there was an attempt to denigrate Calcutta. To denigrate Varanasi was 
the second attempt. 
Madam, we have seen that there has been a severe erosion of values 
in the last fifty years. Can we attribute it to anything else except politics? Can 
we attribute politics to anything else than the Constitution? It is time we 
thought about it. Our most hon. and most respected Member, Mr. Pranab 
Mukherjee, just said about Constitution Revision "Well, we do not know 
what is going to happen". How can you know? You just can't because the 
exercise is yet to be done by the Committee.  I don't know why such panic,

such paranoia, is being shown to this particular aspect of the attempt to amend 
the Constitution. Please wait. There are very remarkable brains in the 
Committee. Mr. Justice Venkatachalaiah, the ex -Chief Justice of India, is 
presiding over it. With him there and with so many other luminaries of the 
country there, why are you feeling scared? Let them come up with some 
positive recommendations. This House is still there to discuss with them. You 
can throw it out. Who prevents you? If it is not worthy of being adopted, this 
House can easily throw it out. Where is the point in making such a hullabaloo 
about it as if the heavens are falling. But this is the kind of paranoia the 
Opposition parties showed right across the country. They have tried to say that 
this amendment is nothing but an insult to Dr. Ambedkar. Now our friend Mr. 
Pradhan, the other day quoted from the proceedings of the Constituent 
Assembly or of the Rajya Sabha that Dr. Ambedkar himself in September 1952 
said that this Constitution should be burned up. Then somebody asked him in 
March, 1953 as to why he said this? He said, I am happy that I got this 
opportunity to tell you why I wanted this. "It is because we framed this 
Constitution, this political temple so that we could put a God in it. But before 
the God could come in, this has already been overtaken by the devil. " These 
are the words which have been quoted by hon. Member Shri Pradhan. And 
then, outside, all over the country, parades and rallies were organised as 
though this Constitution is aimed at almost doing away with the Scheduled 
Castes altogether. Madam, I want to put this on record that it is the BJP who 
has fielded the maximum number of SC candidates and made the maximum 
number of SC candidates win and come to Parliament in this century, in the 
present Parliament. And they say that they are trying to do so. This is the vote 
bank politics - that is denigrating every single act that the BJP does and just 
because they think that they can get half a miles or quarter of a mile of 
political mileage in it. This is the lowness of political activity , Madam. 
Lastly, I would come to the point of erosion in values that have taken place in 
this country. The corruption levels, the absence of int egrity, etc. I remember 
here in this House I said, it looks immoral for Members of Parliament to order 
for rise in their own salaries. It is totally immoral for Members themselves to 
take up a Resolution on raising their own salaries. There should have bee n a 
machinery which would have done this according to certain principles, certain 
norms. But Parliamentarians raised their salaries on their own. I did 
recommend to the House that for those days, when Parliament does not 
function, Members

should automatically be deprived of the daily allowance that they draw on

Parliamentary work was stopped and yet every Member received his daily 
allowance for th ose days also. I hope and believe and at least my leader has

this country. It was they who set in the ball of corruption. In fact, if I would 
say so, it is the press which is responsible, in the first insta nce, to create a 
feeling when it described the 15th of August or 16th of August as a day of 
'transfer of power.' Madam, in Hindi we say हमने इस पद का कायर्भार संभाला ।  
For us, in our culture, every job is a burden to carry. But here they ' describe as 
'transfer of POWER'. Now that power point got stuck in the minds of the then 
rulers of this country and they started searching where the power is. Madam, 
power is not power in the sense, the world understands power, until it is 
misused. I recall the time when a person, a friend of mine, recommended 
something for one of his relations, who was working under me, in one of the 
districts. I found that I could not do it. So, I told him, sorry, I could not do it. 
Later on, in a Party where a large number of people wer e sitting there his wife 
started complaining. She said, "You have not done my work." I said, "This is 
the problem." Then my friend said  क्या दो कौड़ी क े  डी. आई. जी. हैं । क्या कह रहे 
हैं नहीं कर सकते ? आप दो कौड़ी क े  डी. आई. जी. हैं । When he said it for th e third 
time, a very old man, an officer of the 1939 seniority, who was sitting there, 
shouted at him and said, "Are you aware with whom you are talking?" I told 
him to keep quiet. 1 said, "He is saying the right thing." ये तो दो कौड़ी का आंकते 
हैं हमको । हम तो एक कौड़ी क े  भी नहीं हैं । 
 
Madam, power is not power until it is misused. Therefore, I would 
like to draw the attention of the nation to this aspect. The Constitution should 
be so made that this kind of misuse of power is stopped. That is all. Thank you.

SHRI CHO S. RAMASWAMY (Nominated): Sir, the hon. President 
has expressed confidence that there is a distinct upturn in the economic 
situation and that efforts are on to bring the fruits of reform to those sections 
which had been ignored. But there are many voices of protest even in the 
ruling alliance. There is dissidence on liberalisation, privatisation and 
globalisation. And I do not know what is going to happen. If not now, at least, 
later on, this Government and the successive Governments would be forced to 
change track, and, in my opinion, it will be a tragedy because we are not giving 
anything a fair trial. We tried socialism. We abandoned it in the middle.  Now, 
we are trying market economy. But because of protests, because of voices of 
dissent, I do not know what is going to happen to it. I am reminded of a 
popular story. A man was given a punishment by a local panchayat. He was 
given three options - take 100 chillies or take 100 onions or surrender all his 
money, all his savings, and go back as a pauper. This man agreed to take 100 
chillies, and he started taking them. But, by about 80 chillies, he found it very 
difficult; his stomach started burning; his eyes 
 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [ 24 April, 2000] 
started watering. So, he said, "No, I will not take this chilli treatment, but I 
will take the onion treatment." Then, he started with the onions. But, half way 
through, he found it difficult; his stomach started cry ing for help. So, he said, 
"I don't want this onion treatment either. I will surrender all my money and go 
back as a pauper." Likewise, we took the chilli treatment first - socialism. We 
found it hard. We found it impossible. So, we abandoned it in the middle. 
Then, we started taking the onion treatment, that is, market economy. Let us 
continue with it. Let us not go back totally ruined, by giving it up in the 
middle. But, at the same time, care has to be taken to see to it that the less -
privileged are taken  proper care of. Food subsidy is an item which, in my 
opinion, has to be retained. In the United States, there is health care. In our 
country, I consider food subsidy as a health care because it supplies the basic 
need for the poor of this country. They ar e being asked to make sacrifices by 
taking rice supplied through the PDS. They are making a sacrifice already 
because the quality of rice is so bad. So, asking them to make a double 
sacrifice and pay a higher price is not fair. We would require the cooperation 
of all the people, particularly, the less privileged people, in order to make 
liberalisation a success. Therefore, I feel that we could call it our health care 
programme. That way, perhaps, we would be able to convince even the 
international institutions. 
On Constitution review, it was suggested that persons who were 
prepared to cut off limbs are now objecting to obtaining a medical report. I 
agree with the idea. It is illogical to say, "conduct any number of operations; 
let there be any number of surg eries, but don't have an overall medical report 
before you do anything." I find this illogical. At the same time, I have my own 
reservations whether it is the right time for a review of the Constitution. When 
the Constitution was drafted, the country was e xperiencing a great pride in the 
newly acquired sovereignty. There was unity amongst all sections of the 
people, all varieties of people, all shades of opinion. Divisive forces had gone 
to the corner. They were totally ignored. And the leaders were such th at they 
inspired confidence in every single Indian. But, now, the situation is totally 
different. When we are going to review the Constitution made during those 
times, the time must be as conducive as that for a review. Now there are 
divisive forces. What will be the demands that would come forth? The 
demands will be based on regional chauvinism, on language fanaticism, on 
casteism. There will be demands for dilution of the independence of the 
judiciary.   There will be demands with an eye on the 
 
246 

[24 April, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
communal vote. To avoid all these things, I think, it will be better not to 
indulge in this exercise now. But nothing is going to happen because of the 
appointment of the Commission. There will be no great danger to the 
Constitution. No amendment is going to be made by the Commission. After 
all, it is the Parliament which has to amend the Constitution. No doubt, the 
Commission consists of eminent persons - persons of unimpeachable 
character, integrity, intelligence and experience. S o, one need not be afraid of 
the work of the Commission. But the main objection is whether the time is 
conducive for this exercise. 
Sir, coming to the third point, the President has expressed his 
confidence that by the year 2001, all children between the ages of 6 and 14 in 
this country would be going to schools. As I said in a different context, this is 
the triumph of hope over experience. Let us think why our people, the rural 
folk, the under -privileged, the poverty -stricken people of this country, are 
refusing to send their children to schools. It is because they cannot afford to 
feed a mouth which is not productive. A child must become productive even 
at the age of five or six if the family is to survive. 
That is why they are not sending their children t o school. We should 
take an entirely different attitude towards education of the lesser -privileged 
classes. We should first ask ourselves; are these children living in such 
conditions which are conducive for learning, for getting educated and so on? 
You have slums, ill- provided villages, families which gamble, familes which 
indulge in illicit distillation. This is the atmosphere in which these children 
live. How can they learn in this atmosphere and achieve parity with the other 
classes of people? So, in my  opinion, these children must be given the best of 
education and, that too, in residential schools. All over the country, on a war -
footing, residential schools must be started for the poorest of the poor. Well, it 
would entail expenditure. But one could at tack the other spheres -intensify 
disinvestment, intensify the efforts to reduce the strength of bureaucracy. But 
whatever money is spent on this programme would be well -spent. It is as 
important as spending money on defence. The parents could be asked to visit 
the children once in a fortnight or once in a month. They would be provided 
with a few sets of uniform; a thatched shed with an asbestos' roofing would do. 
By providing residential accommodation and food and education, definitely, I 
think, in about 1 5 years, the entire scenario of the country would have 
undergone a remarkable change.

I am disappointed, Sir, that the President has not referred to the 
problems being faced in sharing of the waters between different Sta tes. Tamil 
Nadu, for example, is still to reach an agreement with Karnataka on Kavery. 
The Prime Minister, recently, a couple of days back, has referred to drought in 
two States and he has asked the entire nation to help. He is very right. But 
should a Sta te be affected by drought before other States are prepared to 
cooperate with it? For twenty years, Kavery talks have been going on. For 
several years now, the State Government has been saying that it will be 
receiving the Krishna waters for the drinking purposes of Madras city. Lord 
Krishna may come, but we do not know whether the Krishna water will come 
or not! That seems to be the situation. What is the role of the national parties? 
The national parties in both the States take different stances in the Sta tes. In 
Karnataka, they say, "No Tribunal. No Water". In Tamil Nadu, they say, 
"Obey the Tribunal's order; give water to Tamil Nadu". Is this not hypocritical 
on the part of the national parties? On the part of the regional parties, I am 
able to understand this. I could understand a regional party in Tamil Nadu 
taking one view and a regional party in Karnataka taking another view. But 
both the main national parties, the BJP and the Congress, are guilty of this. 
They take one view in Karnataka and another vi ew in Tamil Nadu. I don't 
know how they become national by taking two different views, to suit their 
regional purposes, to vie with the regional parties there. There must be a 
solution to the water-sharing problem. A State need not be affected by drought 
before other States are willing to cooperate with it. 
Finally, I personally feel that the President's Address is a ceremony; 
the Parliament's Motion of Thanks is a formality, and the Members support is 
a gesture. I make this gesture. I support the Motion. Thank you.

STATEMENT BY MINISTER 
Match-fixing in Cricket 
THE MINISTER OF YOUTH AFFAIRS AND SPORTS (SHRI 
SUKHDEV SINGH DHINDSA): Sir, Government is seriously alarmed by the 
recent revelations regarding match-fixing in cricket, specially in the context of 
the recently concluded series betwee n India and South Africa. The Delhi 
Police, on the basis of information in its possession, has ledged FIR No.l 
11/2000 in this connection against Mr. Hansie Cronje and others. Keeping in 
view, these developments, the Department of Sports summoned all the 
concerned agencies and officials, to get an insight into the various facts of this 
particular case. The case is under investigation and the full dimension of this 
problem will only be apparent once the detailed investigation gets completed. 
However, the Department is keeping a watch on developments in this case on 
a regular basis. This investigation will require full support of the persons and 
agencies concerned. The Board for Control of Cricket in India (BCCI) has 
assured that it will extend its complete co -operation in this regard so that the 
culprits could be discovered. They are also agreeable to making the 
Chandrachud Report public. 
Other than the specific FIR registered by the Delhi Police, 
Government does not, at this stage, have any specific complaint  against 
particular Indian cricketers or office - bearers of the Board for Control of 
Cricket in India. Allegations of i general nature are however, being reported in 
the media. Nevertheless, Government will in all seriousness, initiate necessary 
legal meas ures against practices of match -fixing on the basis of specific 
complaints that may be received, after appropriate inquiry and necessary 
investigation. The Government will take recourse to all legal measures to 
ensure that this menace is not only curbed but eliminated. It will not hesitate

that certain persons were being subjected to, and, in the course of that 
investigation, they hit upon the alleged conversation, which is now the 
subject- matter of the public outcry. I am further given to understand that the 
Delhi Police, instead of reporting these facts to the Ministry of Home Affairs, 
informed the Ministry of External Affa irs that, in fact, they were going to 
lodge an FIR. They sought no permission, either from the Ministry of Home 
Affairs or from the Ministry of External Affairs, and by the time the External 
Affairs Ministry could inform the next morning the Ambassador of South 
Africa, the FIR had already been lodged. So, it was a fait accompli; in the FIR, 
five South African players were named. What concerns me is the manner in 
which the Delhi Police conducted itself. Mr. Minister, you are aware that this 
has tremendous ra mifications. You are also aware of the fact that the charges 
that are sought to be framed, are under section 420 IPC, read with section 
120B, which is conspiracy. You are also aware of the fact that there is no 
extradition treaty with South Africa, and the  essence of the charge under 
section 420 is a dishonest representation made by A to B for the purposes of 
parting of property of valuable security by B, and thereby, causing loss to A.  
In what manner any representation was made by a South

African player to any member of the Indian public or the Board of Control for

have taken upon themselves the burden of prosecuting t he South African 
Cricketers. What concerns me - as you might know since there is no 
Extradition Treaty -  is that every time a South African Cricketer goes to

extradition of the South African Cricketer back to India to try and send him to

be discharged by the South African Cricket Board is sought to be discharged 
by the Government of India, but to what effect? Can you imagine, Mr.
